sources.title: Letterboxd — Citizen Kane
sources.note: Rating 4.19/5 from 709,064 ratings · 119 min (1941) · directed by Orson Welles.

encyclopedia.summary: Orson Welles directed and starred in this 1941 film and wrote the screenplay with Herman J. Mankiewicz. After the death of the newspaper magnate Charles Foster Kane, a reporter chases the last word he spoke while the accounts of the witnesses contradict one another. Rather than explain one life in a single direction, the film sets out to rebuild it from the memories left behind.

key_facts.value: Herman J. Mankiewicz and Orson Welles
A reporter's interviews cutting across a lifetime

highlights: Shuffling time and layering testimony to rebuild a man became a grammar later films kept borrowing.
Deep-focus photography and sets that showed their ceilings broke studio conventions of the day.
A single last word turns into the device that points at a lifetime of loss.

encyclopedia.summary: Directed by Michael Curtiz in 1942 and adapted from Murray Burnett and Joan Alison's play Everybody Comes to Rick's. In Casablanca under Nazi occupation, Rick runs a bar and finds himself facing the woman who left him, her husband, and a Czech resistance leader at once. The film folds a wartime escape route, a love story and a political choice into a single decision.

key_facts.value: The play by Murray Burnett and Joan Alison
Casablanca, Morocco, during the Second World War

highlights: One bar full of people waiting for passage compresses the whole war's interests.
The song 'As Time Goes By' is remembered together with the film.
The line spoken at the airfield became one of the most quoted in cinema.

encyclopedia.summary: Marjane Satrapi turned her own autobiographical comic into this 2007 animated film with Vincent Paronnaud. A girl grows up through the Iranian revolution and the war with Iraq, moves to Austria and back to Iran, and looks for a voice of her own. Personal history and political history overlap in the same shot throughout.
highlights: Draws revolution and war in black-and-white animation through one girl's memory.
The line of the original comic survives on screen and moves between documentary and fable.
Sees religion and politics entering daily life through an emigrant's eyes.

encyclopedia.summary: Ingmar Bergman's 1966 black-and-white film follows an actress who has stopped speaking and the nurse who cares for her, as the boundary between them erases. It pushes psychology through close-ups and silence rather than dialogue, and turns the film itself into a question aimed at the audience. Among Bergman's mid-period works it is the most radical in form.
highlights: Superimposing the two faces in one frame makes their identification visual.
It opens with film burning through the gate, admitting from the first minute that this is a film.
Later works such as Midsommar and Melancholia inherit this structure of psychological pressure.

related.note: The same director's earlier parable of death and silence

encyclopedia.summary: Elem Klimov's 1985 Soviet film follows a Belarusian boy who picks up a rifle in the woods and joins the partisans. Bombing and massacre are shown only through his eyes, adapted from an account of real events. It is often called the most brutal war film ever made, but the brutality is a matter of viewpoint rather than shock.

key_facts.value: Screenplay drawn from Ales Adamovich's testimony

highlights: Shows a boy's face ageing across a single film's passage of time.
Handles the massacre through sound and gaze so the audience fills it in.
Not the victor's narrative but a record of what one surviving child saw.

related.note: The same era's atrocity through a different gaze
Another film on what war does to a person
